title: Flood Zone Check: FEMA Hazard Context
description: Check a location's flood hazard context with the Flood Zone Check — FEMA flood zone designations explained in plain language. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a home in Zone AE sits in the 1%-annual-chance floodplain — which sounds rare until you compound it: a 26% chance of at least one flood over a 30-year mortgage.
quick_answer: The Flood Zone Check looks up the flood hazard context for a point from FEMA flood map data — the zone designation that insurers, lenders and buyers ask about. Enter the location and read its zone with a plain explanation of what the designation means and what it does not.
steps_intro: Awareness first — the zone, in plain language:

body.t: A zone result starts the right conversations — with the seller, the insurer and the lender — before contracts. It never replaces the official determination those parties will run themselves.
Lenders require flood insurance inside Special Flood Hazard Areas (the A and V zones). Knowing the zone before the quote turns a surprise into a line item.
Lenders and insurers write in zone codes (AE, X, VE). This page translates the code on your letter into ground truth about the land.
Builders and buyers screening several parcels can rank flood context early — formal study stays with engineers, as the
's terrain view complements but never replaces.

Zone AE means a 1% chance of flooding in any year — the so-called 100-year flood. Over a 30-year mortgage that compounds to about a 26% chance of at least one flood (1 − 0.99³⁰). '100-year' describes a probability, not a schedule.

Zone X (shaded) is the 0.2%-annual-chance area — a 5.8% chance over 30 years, outside the mandatory-purchase zone but not outside risk. Unshaded X sits outside even that. The letter is the same; the shading is the story.

popular_table.note: Zones come from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Maps via the National Flood Hazard Layer. Maps get revised; a property's official status is decided by the current effective FIRM and any Letters of Map Change — not by any website, including this one.

faq: Is a zone the whole risk story?

No — zones describe riverine and coastal flooding from the mapped study. Intense local rain, drainage failures and new development flood 'safe' zones regularly; a large share of US flood claims historically come from outside the high-risk zones.
What is a base flood elevation?
The computed height floodwater is expected to reach in the 1% annual event (BFE). Structures' lowest floors are compared against it — the number elevation certificates exist to record.

Yes — restudies, new development and map revisions move boundaries, and a property can be mapped in or out over the years (with formal Letters of Map Change for individual lots). Always argue from the current effective map.
My lender says insurance is required but my check says Zone X.

The lender's determination (run through a certified flood determination company against the effective FIRM) governs your loan. Treat any mismatch as a prompt to request the determination's map panel details, not as a verdict either way.

A high house in a low zone can still flood at the road and the septic field; a low house can be protected by local grading. Elevation informs risk — the Elevation Finder supplies it — but the zone plus the structure's own survey is the formal answer.
Zones matter to renters too: contents coverage is separate from the landlord's policy, and the zone tells you what your belongings are sitting in.
FEMA's system is American. Other countries run their own hazard maps (the UK's Environment Agency flood maps, for instance) with different categories — this page speaks FEMA's language only.

The National Flood Hazard Layer is updated as maps become effective — some counties' studies are recent, others decades old. The check reports the zone of record; the map's effective date is part of an official determination.
